title: Porosity, Air-Filled Porosity, and Water-Holding Capacity
objective: Measure the air-water framework of a substrate and explain why the same mix behaves differently in different containers.

terms.definition: Fraction of bulk substrate volume occupied by pores.
Water retained after saturation and free drainage in a specific container.
Pore volume filled with air at container capacity.
Saturated or near-saturated layer retained above the container base by capillary forces.

coreScience: Substrate pores hold either water or gas. Large, connected pores drain readily and replenish oxygen; smaller pores retain water more strongly. Total porosity alone is incomplete because two mixes can have similar total pore volume but very different distributions between air and water.

Container capacity and air space depend on the container as well as the mix. For the same substrate, a taller column generally drains to a lower average water content and more air space than a shallow column. Adding drainage holes improves exit pathways but does not eliminate the capillary water profile.
Particle breakdown, compaction, root growth, biofilms, salts, and decomposition change pore geometry during production. Measurements on a fresh bag do not guarantee end-of-cycle behavior.

At a defined drained state, total porosity is the combined volume fraction of air-filled and water-filled pores. Air-filled porosity at container capacity is not equivalent to total porosity, and retained water at container capacity is not synonymous with water that roots can extract without stress. Drainage, adhesion to particles, matric potential and root distribution all contribute to the useful water-supply range.

The apparent perched-water region occurs because capillary retention opposes gravity in the packed pore network. A fixed substrate in a shallow pot commonly retains a greater average fraction of water after free drainage than the same substrate in a taller pot, even when both have open drainage outlets. Initial wetting, shrink-swell behavior, packing density and preferential flow can change the observed result.

Container-based gravimetric comparisons need clear reference conditions. Saturate a representative sample by a documented method, allow free drainage for a specified interval, weigh the same container, and compare subsequent weight loss under known conditions. Evaporation, plant transpiration, handling and changes in container tare mass must not be mistaken for the same process.
cultivationRelevance: Match particle distribution and container height to irrigation strategy and plant size. Fine seedling media, large finishing containers, and high-frequency drip systems have different requirements.
A practical container test can quantify saturated volume, drained volume, retained water, and air space. Use the same packing method and moisture history for batch comparisons.

Worked comparison: two batches have the same advertised material blend but show different drainage and recovery. Check fill mass, mixing and pre-moistening, container geometry and drainage behavior before concluding that one ingredient caused the difference. Replicate the physical test with standardized packing.

Use a reference empty-pot tare and repeatable drainage interval when tracking container mass. A drying trend can show water loss, but it does not alone demonstrate sufficient oxygen or quantify precisely how much remaining water is physiologically available.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Nominal and measured volume, height, diameter, base shape, and drainage openings.
Lot, blend ratio, initial moisture, packing method, and compaction.
Saturation volume, drained volume, container capacity, air space, and total porosity.
Settling, shrinkage, root filling, channeling, and end-of-cycle retest.
Volume, frequency, runoff, dryback, and spatial uniformity.

Record container volume and height, substrate dry/fill mass or packing density, prewetting method, time at saturation, free-drain interval, captured drainage, post-drain mass, ambient conditions and number of replicates. Report volumetric fractions with the exact test method.

misconceptions: More perlite always means perfect aeration: Particle size, proportion, packing, container, and root growth determine the result.
More drainage holes remove perched water: They improve exit but do not change the substrate's capillary behavior by themselves.
Water-holding capacity is a property of the bag alone: Container geometry and packing affect the measured value.
Total porosity, air-filled porosity and plant-available water are interchangeable: these are distinct properties measured or inferred under specified states and methods.
evidenceLimits: Different laboratories use related but nonidentical physical-property methods. Report the method, container, packing, and units with every value.

Simple drainage and container-mass tests are useful comparisons but are not direct measures of pore-size distribution, oxygen diffusion rate or root-extractable water potential. Cross-container comparisons require standardized packing, wetting and geometry; no single air-space percentage is universally optimal for cannabis.
